**Xi Jinping**
The General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party since 2012 and President since 2013, who succeeded Hu Jintao and leads the party's "Fifth Generation" of leaders. He is a "princeling," the son of revolutionary veteran Xi Zhongxun, and as a young official in 1985 he spent time in Muscatine, Iowa, studying American agriculture. Under him, China has tightened regulation of private business.

**Zero-COVID policy ("Dynamic Clearing")**
China's strict pandemic strategy, officially called "dynamic zero" or "dynamic clearing," which used mass lockdowns, quarantine camps, and constant PCR testing, often requiring a negative test within 72 hours to go out in public. Shanghai's harsh 2022 lockdown inspired viral online protest content, and China abruptly abandoned the policy in December 2022, after which the U.S. and EU required negative tests from Chinese travelers.

**A4 / White Paper protests and the Urumqi fire**
In November 2022, a deadly apartment fire in Urumqi, Xinjiang, which killed at least 10 people and was blamed on COVID lockdown measures, set off nationwide protests. Demonstrators held up blank sheets of A4 paper to symbolize censorship. Earlier, in October 2022, a lone protester on Beijing's Sitong Bridge hung banners calling Xi a "despotic traitor" and broadcast "we want to eat, we want freedom, we want to vote" on a loudspeaker.

**Uyghurs and Xinjiang**
China has detained an estimated one million or more Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities in "re-education" camps in Xinjiang, drawing accusations of crimes against humanity and genocide. In December 2020, the U.S. banned cotton imports from the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps (XPCC), a paramilitary conglomerate linked to forced labor.

**Huawei and Meng Wanzhou**
Huawei, China's telecom giant, makes chips through its subsidiary HiSilicon. Its CFO Meng Wanzhou, daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei, was arrested in Vancouver in 2018 at U.S. request on charges related to violating Iran sanctions and spent nearly three years under house arrest in Canada before a 2021 deal let her return to China.

**TikTok and ByteDance**
TikTok is the short-video app owned by Beijing-based ByteDance. In 2020 the Trump administration tried to force a sale of its U.S. operations, and a proposed deal with Oracle and Walmart stalled. India, after a deadly 2020 border clash with China, banned TikTok along with more than 200 other Chinese apps.

**Alibaba and Ant Group**
Alibaba, the e-commerce giant founded by Jack Ma, set a record with its roughly $25 billion IPO on the New York Stock Exchange in 2014. It turned "Singles' Day" on November 11 into the world's biggest shopping event. In November 2020, regulators halted the planned record IPO of its financial affiliate Ant Group days before launch, after Ma publicly criticized financial regulators.

**Tencent and WeChat**
Tencent is the Shenzhen-based tech giant behind the messaging app QQ and the "super-app" WeChat (Weixin), which combines messaging, social media, and payments. Its digital "red envelopes" (hongbao), a version of the traditional gift of money in red packets, compete with Alibaba's Alipay.

**Evergrande and the property crisis**
Evergrande, once China's second-largest property developer, defaulted on huge debts in 2021 and became the symbol of a broader real estate collapse. Other unfinished projects were also abandoned, and in 2021 Kunming demolished 15 incomplete high-rises at the stalled Sunshine City II development.

**Hong Kong protests and Carrie Lam**
In 2019, mass protests in Hong Kong against an extradition bill that would have allowed suspects to be sent to mainland China grew into a broader pro-democracy movement against Chief Executive Carrie Lam. Groups like Joshua Wong's Demosisto took part, and protesters used laser pointers against police cameras and followed a "do not split" principle of unity between peaceful and militant factions. These protests came five years after the 2014 Umbrella Movement.

**Taiwan and the "One China" policy**
Taiwan (officially the Republic of China) is the self-governing island that Beijing claims as its territory. In December 2016, President-elect Donald Trump angered Beijing by taking a congratulatory phone call from Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen of the Democratic Progressive Party, breaking with decades of U.S. practice. Taiwan's Kuomintang, which imposed martial law and the "White Terror," replaced its 2016 presidential candidate Hung Hsiu-chu with Eric Chu shortly before the election.

**Senkaku Islands and relations with Japan**
China and Japan dispute the uninhabited Senkaku Islands (Diaoyu in Chinese) in the East China Sea, where Chinese coast guard ships regularly enter waters Japan controls. China banned Japanese seafood imports after Japan began releasing treated water from the Fukushima nuclear plant in 2023. Long-running disputes include Japanese officials' visits to the Yasukuni Shrine, which honors war criminals among Japan's war dead, and how Japanese textbooks portray the Rape of Nanking.

**Bo Xilai and Neil Heywood**
Bo Xilai was the charismatic Chongqing party chief and a rising princeling whose career collapsed in 2012 after his wife, Gu Kailai, was convicted of poisoning British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was sentenced to life in prison in 2013 for bribery, embezzlement, and abuse of power.

**Chen Guangcheng**
A blind, self-taught legal activist who exposed forced abortions under the One-Child Policy. In April 2012 he escaped house arrest in Shandong and took refuge in the U.S. Embassy in Beijing, and he later moved to the United States.

**Deng Xiaoping's "cat theory" and Special Economic Zones**
Deng, China's leader after Mao, justified his market reforms with the saying "It doesn't matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice." His reforms created Special Economic Zones such as Shenzhen and Hainan, and later Shanghai's Pudong New Area, to attract foreign investment.
